intro: Rachmaninoff plays his 1892 Prelude in a 1919 Edison recording, moving from a slow opening through an agitated middle to an enlarged return. What changes when the opening material spreads across a much wider chordal texture?
question: What makes the same opening sound larger on its return?

sections.label: Tempo primo · enlarged return
sections.mNote: opening signal enlarged into doubled chords across widely separated registers

cues.title: Three notes and an answer
cues.text: The opening’s low A–G♯–C♯ figure is set against quieter answering chords. Listen for the contrast between strongly projected notes and the softer lines around them; the score gives both roles to a single pianist.
cues.evidence: The Mutopia score specifies the three-note figure and answering chords; the old recording’s pitch estimates are not used to identify individual notes.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Nineteen and newly qualified
cues.text: Rachmaninoff wrote the Prelude in 1892, the year he graduated from the Moscow Conservatory. It was published as the second of five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3, dedicated to his teacher Anton Arensky.
cues.evidence: The Prelude’s publication history dates its composition to 1892 and the five-piece set to 1893, with the dedication to Arensky.

cues.title: Inside the chords
cues.text: Listen inside the quieter texture rather than following only the highest notes. Voicing means giving simultaneous notes different weights, so that a melodic line remains distinct within the surrounding harmony.
cues.evidence: This is a guide to the score’s chordal piano writing, not an identification of an individual voice from the audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Siloti takes it abroad
cues.text: Alexander Siloti included the Prelude in his 1898 tour of Western Europe and the United States. Publishers subsequently marketed it under descriptive titles, including The Burning of Moscow and The Day of Judgement, rather than the composer’s plain key-and-genre title.
cues.evidence: The Prelude’s reception history records Siloti’s tour and the titles used by London publishers.

cues.title: Motion in the agitated middle
cues.text: The middle section’s triplet movement gathers force towards the opening material’s return. Listen through the rapid figures for the melodic notes, distinguishing their line from the increased number of attacks.
cues.evidence: The score marks an Agitato middle; rising activity around 1:45–2:15 locates its build-up, not its first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening, enlarged
cues.text: The return presents the opening material in a broad chordal texture. Rachmaninoff spreads the notation across four staves, two for each hand: the added space separates registers and lines, not additional players.
cues.evidence: The Mutopia score shows the four-stave return; reduced attack activity around 2:18–2:20 supports its approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer at the keyboard
cues.text: Commons identifies this as Rachmaninoff’s 1919 Edison recording, issued in December 1920 on Diamond Disc 82187-R. It credits Adam Cuerden with cleaning and restoring this digital copy.
cues.evidence: The Commons source page distinguishes recording and issue dates, identifies the disc and names the restorer.

cues.title: After the weight
cues.text: The coda retreats from the enlarged return into softer, more widely spaced chords. Follow the line through the fading resonance: the strongest passage is not the last thing the piece has to say.
cues.evidence: The score ends with a quiet coda; the relative level declines markedly across 3:15–3:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass arrives; the upper line moves
transitions.how: The Lento’s last bass gestures repeat A–G♯ and settle on C♯ as the Agitato begins. There is no new tonic: C♯ minor remains underneath the change from separated chords to continuous triplets. Above that held bass, the melody descends E–D♯–D♮–C♯, its chromatic steps embedded in the moving chords. Faster surface motion and the new tempo release the tension of the opening’s pauses without abandoning its harmonic ground.
transitions.evidence: The 1:46 section boundary is the strongest analysis change; level rises sharply after the quiet 1:40 window and activity increases into 1:55. Mutopia’s score, bars 13–16, supplies the A–G♯–C♯ bass connection, held C♯ and descending chromatic melody. The historical transfer is not used to identify those notes or an exact bar onset.

transitions.title: The running chords become the opening signal
transitions.how: The triplet chords drive into two massive bass notes, A and G♯, before C♯ completes the opening’s three-note signal. Their harmony makes the route explicit: F♯ minor over A, then G♯ dominant seventh, then C♯ minor. The running texture stops and Tempo primo restores the broad pace, but the opening now fills widely separated registers in heavy, doubled chords. The return is prepared by a cadence and by the bass motif itself, not just announced by greater volume.
transitions.evidence: The 2:18 section boundary lies among strong changes at 2:14, 2:18 and 2:22; attack density falls from 4.8 per second near 2:15 to 0.8 near 2:20. Mutopia bars 44–46 show A with F♯-minor harmony, G♯ with dominant-seventh harmony and the C♯-minor Tempo primo return across four staves. The span includes the preparatory bass notes.

transitions.title: The bass stops travelling
transitions.how: After the enlarged theme, the bass reaches C♯ and stays there through the coda. The upper chords keep changing chromatically over this tonic pedal; their colour changes no longer require the bass to find a new destination. Widely spaced attacks replace the return’s crowded, emphatic chords, and the dynamic falls. Only at the end do the upper voices settle into plain C♯ minor: the tonic bass is secured before the harmony above it comes to rest.
transitions.evidence: The 3:12 section boundary has a strong analysis change, followed by declining level from approximately −12.4 dB at 3:10 to −18.6 dB at 3:15 and much lower values later. Mutopia bars 56–62 show the repeated or tied C♯ bass octaves, changing upper harmonies and final C♯-minor chord. No chord is identified from the old recording’s key estimates.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
